Modeling 08: Vulnerability Index and SWOT Synthesis

climasus4r Team

20/09/2026

Source: vignettes/mod-08-vulnerabilidade-swot.Rmd
mod-08-vulnerabilidade-swot.Rmd

Objective

By the end of this tutorial you will be able to:

  1. Compose a Composite Vulnerability Index (CVI) following the IPCC AR6 three-pillar structure — climate Exposure, population Sensitivity, and Adaptive Capacity — from health-climate, socioeconomic, and health infrastructure indicators, using sus_mod_vulnerability_index();
  2. Interpret the vulnerability ranking across municipalities and measure territorial inequality with the Gini Coefficient and the Lorenz curve;
  3. Synthesize the results into a SWOT analysis (Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities and Threats) oriented toward health-climate public policy, using sus_mod_swot();
  4. Visualize and communicate the results with the paired plotting functions sus_mod_plot_vulnerability() (ranking, pillars, Lorenz) and sus_mod_plot_swot() (radar, 2×2 matrix, bars).

This is the eighth module in the Modeling series of climasus4r. The main inputs are the climasus_af object from Module M2 (mod_af.rds) and the climasus_dlnm object from Module M1 (mod_dlnm_fit.rds). The main output is the climasus_vi object saved as mod_vi.rds for reuse in final reports and risk communication.

Scientific background

Climate vulnerability according to the IPCC

The IPCC’s Fifth Assessment Report (AR5, 2014) established the three-pillar framework that defines vulnerability — later refined in AR6 (2022) — as a function of three interdependent components:

  • Exposure: the degree to which a system or population is affected by climate stressors (extreme temperature, heat waves, days above the 90th percentile of heat);
  • Sensitivity: the level of response of a system to the stressor, conditioned by intrinsic factors such as the proportion of elderly people, prevalence of chronic disease, and the dose-response relationship estimated by DLNM models;
  • Adaptive Capacity: the set of institutional, economic, and infrastructural resources that allow a system to modulate its impacts (human development index, treated water coverage, density of primary health care units).

The composite index formula, originally proposed by Turner et al. (2003) and adopted in the social vulnerability literature (Cutter, Boruff & Shirley, 2003; Benmarhnia et al., 2015), inverts the Adaptive Capacity pillar before combination, since higher capacity means lower vulnerability:

VIi=wE⋅Ei+wS⋅Si+wAC⋅(1−ACi)wE+wS+wAC VI_i = \frac{w_E \cdot E_i + w_S \cdot S_i + w_{AC} \cdot (1 - AC_i)}{w_E + w_S + w_{AC}}

where EiE_i, SiS_i, and ACiAC_i are the weighted averages of the normalized indicators (min-max or z-score) of municipality ii for each pillar, and wEw_E, wSw_S, wACw_{AC} are the inter-pillar weights. Missing indicators are handled through automatic reweighting.

Min-max and z-score normalization

Min-max normalization projects each indicator xijx_{ij} onto the interval [0,1][0, 1]:

x̃ij=xij−minj(xij)maxj(xij)−minj(xij) \tilde{x}_{ij} = \frac{x_{ij} - \min_j(x_{ij})}{\max_j(x_{ij}) - \min_j(x_{ij})}

Z-score normalization standardizes by mean and standard deviation, preserving the original distribution — useful when indicators have very heterogeneous scales, but it requires a back-transformation for direct interpretation.

Territorial inequality and the Lorenz Curve

The Lorenz Curve is the classic instrument for visualizing the concentration of any resource or burden across an ordered population. In the context of climate risk, the curve accumulates the proportion of total CVI (y-axis) against the proportion of municipalities (x-axis), from least to most vulnerable. The larger the area between the curve and the diagonal of perfect equality, the higher the Gini Coefficient — which ranges from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (all risk concentrated in a single municipality).

Climate risk concentration analyses have been applied at multi-city scale by Gasparrini et al. (2017) and in national socio-environmental vulnerability studies in Brazil by Confalonieri et al. (2009) and Marengo et al. (2022).

SWOT analysis oriented toward health-climate policy

The SWOT framework (Andrews, 1971), widely used in strategic planning, has been adapted to climate-health risk management. In this approach:

  • Strengths (S) represent existing protective factors — high adaptive capacity, low total attributable fraction;
  • Weaknesses (W) reflect current vulnerabilities — high population sensitivity, high heat- and cold-attributable fractions;
  • Opportunities (O) identify windows for intervention — municipalities with a relatively low vulnerability index and moderate current exposure have room to advance prevention before reaching critical levels;
  • Threats (T) signal emerging or already present risks — high climate exposure, high relative heat risk (DLNM), high attributable number.

Data used

Object Source Content
caso_espacial.rds Tutorial T5 sf geometries of the RMSP municipalities
caso_socio.rds Tutorial T6 Socioeconomic indicators per municipality (HDI, % elderly, etc.)
mod_dlnm_fit.rds Module M1 climasus_dlnm object fitted for the RMSP
mod_af.rds Module M2 climasus_af object with total/heat/cold AF%

Whenever any of these four files is missing (execution outside the full chain), the pre-rendering script synthesizes realistic data with a warning — the Rmd renders normally, displaying illustrative results.

Complete pipeline 

library(climasus4r)
library(dplyr)

Load chained inputs 

# Objeto climasus_af do Módulo M2
mod_af <- if (file.exists("vignettes-pt/dados/mod_af.rds")) {
  readRDS("vignettes-pt/dados/mod_af.rds")
} else {
  NULL  # fallback: SWOT rodará sem AF
}

# Objeto climasus_dlnm do Módulo M1
mod_dlnm <- if (file.exists("vignettes-pt/dados/mod_dlnm_fit.rds")) {
  readRDS("vignettes-pt/dados/mod_dlnm_fit.rds")
} else {
  NULL  # fallback: sem extração DLNM automática
}

# Indicadores socioeconômicos
caso_socio <- if (file.exists("vignettes-pt/dados/caso_socio.rds")) {
  readRDS("vignettes-pt/dados/caso_socio.rds")
} else {
  # Mínimo realista para o script funcionar sem a cadeia completa
  data.frame(
    city          = c("Sao Paulo", "Guarulhos", "Santo Andre", "Osasco", "Maua"),
    pct_idosos    = c(16.2, 12.4, 14.8, 13.1, 11.9),
    pct_doenca_cr = c(28.1, 24.3, 26.7, 22.8, 20.5),
    hdi           = c(0.845, 0.763, 0.815, 0.776, 0.742),
    pct_agua      = c(97.2, 88.4, 94.1, 90.3, 85.7),
    densidade_ubs = c(6.8, 3.2, 5.1, 4.0, 2.9)
  )
}

Build the three IPCC pillars

Each pillar is supplied as a data.frame with a municipal identifier column (city_col = "city") and numeric indicator columns. Indicators missing for a given municipality are filled with NA and excluded from the pillar’s weighted average, without forcing complete exclusion.

# ----- Pilar E: Exposição Climática ------------------------------------------
# Fonte: sus_climate_aggregate() (temperatura maxima media, dias de calor P90,
#        contagem de ondas de calor por ano)
exposure_df <- data.frame(
  city           = caso_socio$city,
  tmax_media     = c(29.8, 31.2, 28.9, 30.1, 31.8),  # grau Celsius
  dias_calor_p90 = c(52,   68,   45,   58,   72),     # dias/ano
  ondas_calor    = c(4,    8,    3,    6,    9)        # eventos/ano
)

# ----- Pilar S: Sensibilidade Populacional -----------------------------------
# Fonte: caso_socio.rds + extração automática de climasus_dlnm (argumento fits)
sensitivity_df <- caso_socio[, c("city", "pct_idosos", "pct_doenca_cr")]

# ----- Pilar AC: Capacidade Adaptativa ---------------------------------------
# Fonte: caso_socio.rds (HDI, cobertura hídrica, densidade UBS)
adaptive_capacity_df <- caso_socio[, c("city", "hdi", "pct_agua", "densidade_ubs")]

Fit the Composite Vulnerability Index

sus_mod_vulnerability_index() accepts a fits argument (a named list of climasus_dlnm objects) for automatic extraction of the metrics dlnm_hot_rr, dlnm_cold_rr, and dlnm_sensitivity_index, which are automatically merged into the sensitivity pillar.

# Opcional: lista nomeada de climasus_dlnm (um por cidade)
# fits_dlnm <- list(sao_paulo = mod_dlnm)  # ajuste por municipio

vi_fit <- sus_mod_vulnerability_index(
  exposure_df          = exposure_df,
  sensitivity_df       = sensitivity_df,
  adaptive_capacity_df = adaptive_capacity_df,
  fits                 = NULL,                # ou: fits_dlnm (lista climasus_dlnm)
  city_col             = "city",
  normalize            = "minmax",            # "minmax" ou "zscore"
  weights              = c(tmax_media = 2,    # dobrar peso da Tmax
                           pct_idosos = 2),   # dobrar peso da proporção de idosos
  pillar_weights       = c(exposure         = 1.5,
                           sensitivity      = 1.0,
                           adaptive_capacity = 1.0),
  hot_percentile       = 0.99,
  cold_percentile      = 0.01,
  lang                 = "pt",
  verbose              = TRUE
)

# Inspecionar o resultado
print(vi_fit)

The climasus_vi object contains:

Element Type Content
$vi_table tibble CVI, pillar scores, rank, and percentile per city
$pillar_scores tibble (long) Raw scores for the three pillars per city
$normalized_indicators tibble Normalized indicators (prefixes exp_, sen_, ac_)
$raw_indicators tibble Original indicators without normalization
$weights list Intra-pillar and inter-pillar weights effectively used
$gini_coefficient numeric Gini of the CVI (0 = perfect equality)
$meta list Call parameters, counts, timing

Fit the SWOT Analysis

sus_mod_swot() aggregates climasus objects from multiple modules into normalized (0–100) and categorized SWOT quadrants. The argument breaks = c(25, 50, 75) produces four categories (Low / Medium / High / Very High) — the default c(33, 66) produces three categories.

swot_fit <- sus_mod_swot(
  vulnerability = vi_fit,
  af            = mod_af,    # climasus_af do Módulo M2 (ou NULL)
  burden        = NULL,      # climasus_burden do Módulo M2 (opcional)
  dlnm          = mod_dlnm,  # climasus_dlnm do Módulo M1 (broadcast)
  sensitivity   = NULL,      # climasus_sensitivity do Módulo M7 (opcional)
  score_type    = "both",    # "numeric", "categorical" ou "both"
  breaks        = c(25, 50, 75),
  labels        = c("Baixo", "Médio", "Alto", "Muito Alto"),  # 4 cats para 3 breaks
  city_col      = "city",
  lang          = "pt",
  verbose       = TRUE
)

# Visualizar tabela de escores
swot_fit$scores

Function characteristics

sus_mod_vulnerability_index() — IPCC Vulnerability Index

Full signature:

sus_mod_vulnerability_index(
  exposure_df          = NULL,
  sensitivity_df       = NULL,
  adaptive_capacity_df = NULL,
  fits                 = NULL,
  city_col             = "city",
  normalize            = "minmax",
  weights              = NULL,
  pillar_weights       = c(exposure = 1, sensitivity = 1, adaptive_capacity = 1),
  hot_percentile       = 0.99,
  cold_percentile      = 0.01,
  lang                 = "pt",
  verbose              = TRUE
)

Key parameters:

Argument Type Description
exposure_df data.frame Indicators for the Exposure pillar (higher = more exposed)
sensitivity_df data.frame Indicators for the Sensitivity pillar (higher = more sensitive)
adaptive_capacity_df data.frame Indicators for the Adaptive Capacity pillar (higher = more adapted)
fits named list of climasus_dlnm Automatic extraction of heat/cold RR and sensitivity index
city_col character Name of the municipal identifier column (default "city")
normalize "minmax" or "zscore" Indicator normalization method
weights named vector Intra-pillar weights by column name; unlisted columns get weight 1
pillar_weights named vector c(exposure, sensitivity, adaptive_capacity) Inter-pillar weights; missing pillars automatically get weight 0
hot_percentile / cold_percentile numeric Quantiles for RR extraction from the DLNM fits

Return — climasus_vi object:

  • $vi_table: tibble ordered by vi_rank (rank 1 = most vulnerable), with columns vi_score ∈ [0, 1], exposure_score, sensitivity_score, adaptive_capacity_score, vi_rank, vi_percentile.
  • $pillar_scores: long tibble with city, pillar, score (raw score before the AC inversion).
  • $normalized_indicators / $raw_indicators: wide tibbles with prefixes exp_, sen_, ac_.
  • $weights: list with the intra-pillar and inter-pillar weights effectively used.
  • $gini_coefficient: Gini of the CVI distribution.
  • $meta: list of parameters, counts, and timestamp.

Available S3 methods: print(), summary(), tidy() (returns a flat tibble), coef() (returns a named vector city → vi_score).

sus_mod_plot_vulnerability() — CVI Visualizations

Full signature:

sus_mod_plot_vulnerability(
  x,
  type        = c("ranking", "pillars", "lorenz"),
  output_type = c("plot", "table", "all"),
  interactive = FALSE,
  base_size   = 12L,
  save_plot   = NULL,
  lang        = c("pt", "en", "es"),
  verbose     = FALSE
)

Plot types (type=):

type Description Data returned in "table"
"ranking" Horizontal lollipop: CVI per city, most vulnerable at the top $vi_table
"pillars" Horizontal stacked bars: contribution of E / S / AC per city $pillar_scores
"lorenz" Lorenz curve of CVI inequality with the Gini annotated $vi_table

Return: ggplot (output_type = "plot"), tibble ("table"), or a named list $plot, $table, $data ("all"). With interactive = TRUE, returns a plotly widget (requires the plotly package).

sus_mod_swot() — Climate-Health SWOT Synthesis

Full signature:

sus_mod_swot(
  vulnerability = NULL,
  af            = NULL,
  burden        = NULL,
  dlnm          = NULL,
  sensitivity   = NULL,
  score_type    = c("both", "numeric", "categorical"),
  breaks        = c(33, 66),
  labels        = NULL,
  city_col      = "city",
  lang          = c("pt", "en", "es"),
  verbose       = TRUE
)

Indicators per quadrant:

Quadrant Source Extracted indicators
S Strengths climasus_vi adaptive_capacity_score (high capacity = strength)
S Strengths climasus_af 100 − total AF% (low burden = strength)
S Strengths climasus_burden Inverted burden rank
W Weaknesses climasus_vi sensitivity_score (high sensitivity = weakness)
W Weaknesses climasus_af Heat AF%; cold AF%
W Weaknesses climasus_sensitivity RR inequality across strata
O Opportunities climasus_vi 100 − CVI percentile (low percentile = window); current exposure inverted
T Threats climasus_vi exposure_score; vi_score
T Threats climasus_dlnm Heat RR at P95 (scaled 0–100)
T Threats climasus_burden Normalized attributable number
T Threats climasus_sensitivity Maximum RR across strata

Return — climasus_swot object:

  • $scores: tibble with one row per entity; columns entity, S_score, W_score, O_score, T_score (0–100) and, when score_type %in% c("categorical","both"), S_cat, W_cat, O_cat, T_cat; counts n_S, n_W, n_O, n_T.
  • $indicators: long tibble with one row per (entity × quadrant × indicator): entity, quadrant, ind_code, indicator, raw_value, norm_score, direction ("positive" or "negative").
  • $meta: list with n_entities, n_indicators, inputs_used, score_type, breaks, labels, lang, call_time.

S3 methods: print(), summary(), tidy() (returns $scores).

sus_mod_plot_swot() — SWOT Visualizations

Full signature:

sus_mod_plot_swot(
  x,
  type        = c("radar", "matrix", "bar"),
  output_type = c("plot", "table", "all"),
  interactive = FALSE,
  entities    = NULL,
  top_n       = 3L,
  base_size   = 12L,
  save_plot   = NULL,
  lang        = c("pt", "en", "es"),
  verbose     = FALSE
)

Plot types (type=):

type Description Recommended use
"radar" Spider/radar chart of the four SWOT scores (0–100) per entity, with overlapping polygons for multi-city comparison Comparing profiles across municipalities
"matrix" Classic 2×2 chart: numeric score, category, and bullet points of the leading indicators per quadrant. Shows only one entity (the first in the entities selection) Risk communication for a single municipality
"bar" Grouped horizontal bars of the four SWOT scores per entity Quick comparison across all municipalities

Argument top_n (only for type = "matrix"): maximum number of indicator bullets displayed per quadrant (default 3).

Return: ggplot or plotly (output_type = "plot"), tibble ("table"), or a list $plot, $table ("all").

Reference formulas

Composite Vulnerability Index (IPCC)

The central formula combines the three pillars with the Adaptive Capacity inversion:

VIi=wE⋅Ei+wS⋅Si+wAC⋅(1−ACi)wE+wS+wAC VI_i = \frac{w_E \cdot E_i + w_S \cdot S_i + w_{AC} \cdot (1 - AC_i)}{w_E + w_S + w_{AC}}

where each pillar PiP_i is the weighted average of the normalized indicators:

Pi=∑jωjx̃ij∑jωj P_i = \frac{\sum_j \omega_j \tilde{x}_{ij}}{\sum_j \omega_j}

Missing indicators are excluded and the remaining weights are renormalized, partially preserving municipalities with incomplete data.

Min-max normalization

x̃ij=xij−minj(xij)maxj(xij)−minj(xij) \tilde{x}_{ij} = \frac{x_{ij} - \min_j(x_{ij})}{\max_j(x_{ij}) - \min_j(x_{ij})}

When max⁡j−min⁡j≈0\max_j - \min_j \approx 0 (constant variable), the value is fixed at 0.5 (implemented in .vi_minmax_col()).

Gini Coefficient

Given the vector 𝐯\mathbf{v} of VIiVI_i scores sorted in ascending order:

G=2∑i=1ni⋅vin∑i=1nvi−n+1n G = \frac{2 \sum_{i=1}^{n} i \cdot v_i}{n \sum_{i=1}^{n} v_i} - \frac{n+1}{n}

The Gini is reported in $gini_coefficient and annotated on the type = "ranking" and type = "lorenz" plots.

Illustrated results

Vulnerability ranking

The lollipop chart orders municipalities from most (top) to least vulnerable, with the CVI score on the horizontal axis. The Gini Coefficient in the subtitle quantifies the territorial inequality of vulnerability.

Figure 1. Climate-health vulnerability ranking of the RMSP municipalities. Min-max scores on the x-axis; the municipality at the top = most vulnerable (highest CVI). Gini indicates the concentration of risk across municipalities.

Decomposition of the IPCC pillars

The stacked bars allow identification of which pillar dominates the vulnerability of each municipality: Exposure (red), Sensitivity (blue), or Adaptive Capacity (green). Municipalities with balanced pillars indicate multifactorial risk.

Figure 2. Decomposition of the three IPCC pillar scores by municipality, ordered by total CVI (most vulnerable at the top).

Lorenz curve of vulnerability

The Lorenz curve accumulates the proportion of total CVI (y-axis) as a function of the proportion of municipalities (x-axis), from least to most vulnerable. The farther from the diagonal (perfect equality), the greater the concentration of risk in a few municipalities.

Figure 3. Lorenz curve of the Composite Vulnerability Index in the RMSP. The shaded area between the curve and the diagonal of perfect equality (dashed) is proportional to the Gini Coefficient annotated on the plot.

SWOT profile — Radar

The radar chart shows the four SWOT scores (0–100) for all municipalities simultaneously. Larger polygons (especially in W and T) signal greater fragility; wide polygons in S and O indicate protective assets and intervention opportunities.

Figure 4. SWOT profile by municipality in the RMSP. Axes: Strengths (top), Opportunities (right), Threats (bottom), Weaknesses (left). Scale 0–100.

SWOT 2×2 chart — Most vulnerable municipality

The classic 2×2 chart displays, for the municipality with the highest CVI, the numeric score and category of each quadrant, together with the leading indicators (with normalized score) that contributed the most to each quadrant.

Figure 5. SWOT 2×2 chart for the most vulnerable municipality in the RMSP. An ideal format for risk communication to municipal managers.

SWOT scores — Comparative bars

Figure 6. Grouped SWOT scores by municipality. Allows simultaneous comparison of Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats across all municipalities in the RMSP.
